name: ATSAMD10D14A-MUT
title: SAM D10 Arm Cortex-M0+ microcontrollers, 48 MHz, 8 or 16 KB Flash, 4 KB SRAM, 14 to 24 pins, 1.62 V to 3.63 V
summary: A small low-power 32-bit microcontroller line on the Arm Cortex-M0+ core at up to 48 MHz, run from one 1.62 V to 3.63 V supply, with 8 or 16 KB of Flash and 4 KB of SRAM. It has a six-channel DMA controller and event system, two 16-bit TCs and a 24-bit TCC for PWM and motor control, a calendar RTC, up to three SERCOM serial blocks (USART, SPI, I2C, SMBus/PMBus, LIN slave), a 12-bit 350 ksps ADC, a 10-bit DAC, two comparators and a capacitive touch controller. ATSAMD10D14A-MUT is the 16 KB part in the 24-pin QFN with 22 GPIOs, for -40 °C to 85 °C.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M0+ (r0p1), up to 48 MHz, single-cycle multiplier, Micro Trace Buffer
16 KB Flash (x14) or 8 KB (x13), 4 KB SRAM
1.62 V to 3.63 V on the single VDDIO/IN/ANA pin; 1.2 V core from the internal regulator
22 GPIOs on the 24-pin QFN, 18 on the 20-pin SOIC and WLCSP, 12 on the 14-pin SOIC
12-bit, 350 ksps, up to 10 channels, 1/2x to 16x gain, 13 to 16 bits by oversampling
10-bit 350 ksps DAC; two analog comparators with window mode
up to three SERCOMs, each USART, SPI, I2C to 3.4 MHz, SMBus/PMBus or LIN slave
two 16-bit TCs (8, 16 or 32 bit cascaded), one 24-bit TCC with 8 outputs, 32-bit RTC, WDT, SysTick
PTC, up to 72 mutual-capacitance or 16 self-capacitance channels (QFN)
0.4-32 MHz and 32.768 kHz crystal oscillators, OSC8M, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, DFLL48M, FDPLL96M

tables.title: Errata, silicon revision B
rows: Two back-to-back writes to CRCDATAIN can give a wrong CRC.
Put a NOP between successive CRCDATAIN writes.
NVM CTRLB.MANW resets to 0, so a stray pointer write into the NVM range can write the NVM.
VDDIO leakage is high while external reset is held active.
Keep external reset active as briefly as possible.
On some parts BOD12 can come back on too early when leaving standby, causing a BOD12 reset.
Before standby write 0x00000004 to 0x40000838 to turn BOD12 off; after wake-up write 0x00000006 to the same address to turn it back on.
The SYSTICK calibration value is wrong.
The right calibration value is 0x40000000; load the SysTick RELOAD register from the main clock frequency and the tick period the application needs, not from this value.
With the APB clock stopped and the GCLK running, an APB read of a read-synchronized register hangs the system: CPU and DAP AHB-AP stall and debugging becomes impossible.
Avoid such reads in that clock state; recover by power cycling or by a reset on RESETN.
The voltage regulator's low-power mode does not work above 85 °C.
Keep the regulator in normal mode during standby: set SYSCTRL VREG.RUNSTDBY = 1.
In I2C slave mode a CTRLB write inside the AMATCH or DRDY interrupt handler can reset the state machine.

To set ACKACT to 0 write SERCOM STATUS = 0 then CTRLB = 0; to set it to 1 write STATUS = 0 then CTRLB = SERCOM_I2CS_CTRLB_ACKACT; keep each pair of writes atomic by masking higher-priority interrupts. Write CTRLB in those handlers only to close a transaction; otherwise clear AMATCH by writing 1 to its flag (instead of CTRLB.CMD) and clear DRDY by a DATA access in smart mode or by writing 1 to its flag. In place of CMD = 0x3, clear PREC if set and then write AMATCH to INTFLAG.
After an external XOSC32K failure, neither the RST pin nor a GCLK software reset resets the GCLK generators fed from XOSC32K.
Writing a DFLL register before the DFLL clock is requested can freeze the device.
Clear DFLLCTRL.ONDEMAND before configuring the DFLL.
Reaching the COARSE or FINE limit during locking raises out-of-bounds interrupts even when the final lock values are inside the range.
Enable DFLLOOB only after both DFLLLCKC and DFLLLCKF are set in SYSCTRL INTFLAG.
With the filter on and sensing low level, rising edge or both edges, a false INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] can appear when the EIC is enabled.
After enabling the EIC, clear INTFLAG before enabling interrupts.
I2C SEXTTOEN and MEXTTOEN do not work while CTRLA.LOWTOUT is 0, because GCLK_SERCOM_SLOW is then not requested.
Set CTRLA.LOWTOUT = 1 to use either extend time-out.
In USART auto-baud mode a missing stop bit raises neither ISF nor FERR.
In SPI mode with CTRLB.SSDE and CTRLB.RXEN = 1, a false INTFLAG.SSL can occur.
Enable the SERCOM with RXEN = 0, then set RXEN = 1 in a later write.
In TWI master mode with DBGCTRL.DBGSTOP set, entering debug mode stops the transfer only after the current byte completes (with its interrupt), not at once.
Keep DBGCTRL.DBGSTOP = 0 in TWI master mode.

Advanced capture modes (CAPTMIN, CAPTMAX, LOCMIN, LOCMAX, DERIV0) fail unless every higher channel is also in one of them; for example CC0 = CAPTMIN and CC1 = CAPTMAX with CC2 and CC3 = CAPTEN do not work.
Put basic capture on the lower channels and advanced capture on the upper ones, e.g. CC0 and CC1 = CAPTEN, CC2 = CAPTMIN, CC3 = CAPTMAX.
In RAMP2 mode with fault keep, qualified and restart, a fault at the end of the period in the qualified state can restart the next ramp twice.
Keep faults away from the last and first few cycles of a ramp.
A CCx match does not raise every DMA MCx trigger.
Update CC/CCBUF by DMA on the OVF trigger.
With blanking on, a recoverable fault during the first increment of a rising TCC is not blanked.
In dual-slope mode a retrigger event does not clear the counter.
In two-ramp mode an event comes at the end of each ramp, two per cycle, so EVCTRL.CNTSEL.END cannot mark the end of the full double-ramp cycle.
Writing RUNSTDBY after the TCC is enabled stalls that TCC's APB bus; RUNSTDBY in CTRLA is not enable-protected.
Fault filtering does not work on an inverted fault input.
notes: Silicon revision A was not sampled.

circuits.title: Power supply connection
circuits.description: A single 1.62 V to 3.63 V rail powers the device. The VDDIO, VDDANA and VDDIN supplies all come out on the one VDDIO/IN/ANA pin, and GND and GNDANA on the one GND pin; a capacitor across the rail and ground decouples the supply.

circuits.title: Supply current measurement
circuits.description: A supply feeds the joined VDDIN, VDDANA and VDDIO pins, the single VDDIO/IN/ANA pin, through an ammeter in series.

circuits.title: Power supply decoupling
circuits.description: A 1.62 V to 3.63 V rail feeds VDDIO/IN/ANA. A 100 nF capacitor sits at the pin and a 4.7 µF capacitor across the rail; GND returns to the ground plane.

parts.note: at the supply pin, low ESR

circuits.title: External analog references, two sources
circuits.description: Two external references drive VREFA (PA03) and VREFB (PA04) separately. Each has 4.7 µF at the source and 100 nF at the pin to ground.

circuits.title: External analog reference, one source
circuits.description: One external reference feeds both VREFA (PA03) and VREFB (PA04), with 4.7 µF at the source and 100 nF at each pin.

circuits.title: External reset circuit
circuits.description: RESET (PA28) has a 10 kΩ pull-up to VDD and 100 nF to ground. A push-button pulls it low through 330 Ω, which limits the capacitor's discharge current.

circuits.title: External clock source
circuits.description: An external clock signal drives XIN (PA08); XOUT (PA09) is left open or used as GPIO.

circuits.title: Crystal oscillator
circuits.description: A 0.4 MHz to 30 MHz crystal sits between XIN (PA08) and XOUT (PA09), each side loaded with 15 pF to ground, close to the device.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal without load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal connects straight between XIN32 (PA08) and XOUT32 (PA09), the oscillator's internal load capacitance and the PCB supplying the load.

circuits.title: 32.768 kHz crystal with load capacitors
circuits.description: A 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 (PA08) and XOUT32 (PA09) with 22 pF from each side to ground, for better accuracy and safety factor.

circuits.title: SWCLK pull-up
circuits.description: SWCLK (PA30) is pulled up to VDD through 1 kΩ, where the debugger's clock line connects.

circuits.title: Cortex Debug Connector (10-pin)
circuits.description: A 2 x 5 SWD header: VTref (1) to VDD, SWDIO (2) to PA31, SWDCLK (4) to PA30, RESET (10) to PA28/RST, pins 3 and 5 to ground, and pins 6, 7, 8 and 9 unconnected.

circuits.title: 10-pin JTAGICE3 compatible SWD header
circuits.description: A 2 x 5 header that the JTAGICE3 cable plugs into directly: SWDCLK (1) to PA30, GND (2), VTG (4) to VDD, SWDIO (5) to PA31, RESET (6) to PA28/RST; pins 3, 7, 8, 9 and 10 unconnected.

circuits.title: 20-pin IDC JTAG connector
circuits.description: A 2 x 10 IDC header for debuggers such as SAM-ICE: VTref (1) to VDD, SWDIO (7) to PA31, SWDCLK (9) to PA30, RESET (15) to PA28/RST; even pins 4 to 20 grounded (14 to 20 are the reserved GND* pins); pins 2, 3, 5, 11, 13, 17 and 19 unconnected.
notes: Pins 14, 16, 18 and 20 (GND*) are reserved and may be grounded or left open.

operation.text: SAM D10 is a line of small 32-bit microcontrollers on the Arm Cortex-M0+ core, at up to 48 MHz and 2.46 CoreMark/MHz, in 14-, 20- and 24-pin packages with 8 or 16 KB of Flash and 4 KB of SRAM. Every member shares the same peripheral modules, address map and code, and the pinouts step up from one package to the next, so a design can move within the line or up to the larger SAM D parts.

Two sleep modes are chosen in software. Idle halts the CPU and leaves the rest free to run; standby stops every clock and function except those set to keep going. With SleepWalking a peripheral checks its own wake condition (a threshold crossed, a result ready) so the CPU wakes only when needed, and the Event System passes synchronous and asynchronous events between peripherals even in standby.

Both external crystal oscillators and the internal oscillators can drive the system clock. Clock domains are set up one by one, so each peripheral can run at the rate it needs while the CPU keeps a high frequency.

The two-pin Serial Wire Debug port reprograms the Flash in-system and allows debugging and tracing on chip without disturbing the program. A bootloader in the device may also update the application over any of the communication interfaces.

Processor: Cortex-M0+ at up to 48 MHz with single-cycle hardware multiplier and Micro Trace Buffer. Memories: 8 or 16 KB self-programmable Flash, 4 KB SRAM. System: power-on reset and brown-out detection; internal and external clocks with a 48 MHz DFLL (DFLL48M) and a 48 to 96 MHz fractional PLL (FDPLL96M); external interrupt controller with 8 external interrupts and one non-maskable interrupt; two-pin SWD. Low power: idle and standby, SleepWalking. I/O: up to 22 programmable pins. Supply: 1.62 V to 3.63 V.

Six-channel DMA controller and six-channel Event System. Two 16-bit TCs, each usable as one 16-bit or one 8-bit counter with compare/capture channels, or paired into one 32-bit counter. One 24-bit TCC with up to four compare channels and optional complementary outputs, synchronized PWM patterns across pins, deterministic fault protection, fast decay, adjustable dead time, and dithering that adds up to 5 bits of resolution. 32-bit RTC with clock and calendar, watchdog, CRC-32 generator. Up to three SERCOMs, each a USART (full duplex or one-wire half duplex), I2C up to 3.4 MHz, SMBus/PMBus, SPI or LIN slave. A 12-bit 350 ksps ADC with up to 10 channels, differential or single-ended inputs, 1/2x to 16x gain, automatic offset and gain correction, and hardware oversampling and decimation to 13, 14, 15 or 16 bits. A 10-bit 350 ksps DAC, two analog comparators with a window function, and a Peripheral Touch Controller for up to 72 capacitive touch and proximity channels.
Software tells the variants apart by the DEVSEL field of the DSU Device Identification register (DID.DEVSEL); the low 16 bits of DID carry the die number, die revision and device selection.

After reset each pin is a general-purpose I/O under the PORT. Any pin can instead be given to a peripheral through one of eight functions, A to H: set PINCFGn.PMUXEN (n = 0-31) to one, then pick the function with the odd or even field of PMUXn (PMUXE/PMUXO) in the PORT.

The crystal oscillators sit outside the normal PORT functions; SYSCTRL decides when PA08 and PA09 serve XOSC or XOSC32K. Of the SWD pins only SWCLK (PA30) is a normal PORT function. SWDIO (PA31) is switched in automatically when a debugger is detected by cold- or hot-plugging.

The single VDDIO/IN/ANA pin supplies the I/O lines, OSC8M, XOSC, the internal regulator, the ADC, AC, DAC and PTC, and the 32 kHz oscillators OSCULP32K, OSC32K and XOSC32K, over 1.62 V to 3.63 V. The regulator's 1.2 V output runs the core, memories, peripherals, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M; BOD12 watches it. GND is the only ground pin. PA[7:2] belong to the analog side; PA[9:8] carry XOSC; PA[15:10] and PA[31:16] are digital.
The internal regulator has a normal mode, for when the CPU and peripherals run, and a low-power mode with small static draw that can be used in standby.
One rail of 1.62 V to 3.63 V feeds the device. The VDDIO, VDDANA and VDDIN supplies are tied to the main supply, a capacitor goes from that rail to ground, and GND and GNDANA both go to ground.

The power-on reset that watches VDDIO/IN/ANA needs the supply to rise no slower than a minimum rate, and the rise must not be faster than a maximum rate; both limits are among the electrical characteristics.

The device stays in reset after power-up until the supply has settled everywhere inside. It then runs from 1 MHz: OSC8M divided by eight, fed to generic clock generator 0, which clocks the Power Manager. Some synchronous system clocks run, undivided, from that 1 MHz so software can execute. All other generic clocks are off except GCLK_WDT for the watchdog.
Every I/O pin comes up high-impedance (tri-state).

When reset is released the CPU reads its initial stack pointer and program counter from address 0x00000000, the first location of the internal Flash. The code there is free to configure the clocks and their sources.

Three monitors guard the supply. The POR on VDDIO/IN/ANA is always on, at start-up and in every sleep mode, and resets the whole chip if the supply drops below its threshold. BOD33 watches the 3.3 V supply and is configured in SYSCTRL. BOD12 watches the internal VDDCORE once the device is running; its calibration is set in production and kept in the NVM User Row, and must be left unchanged when the user row is rewritten.

Internal high-speed Flash and internal high-speed RAM with one-cycle access at full clock rate, plus a Flash area set aside for EEPROM emulation. The high-speed bus is a bus matrix whose addresses are fixed and never remapped, boot included.
The NVM User Row holds configuration read automatically at power-on, at address 0x804000. It is written through NVMCTRL, and new values reach the other modules only after the next device reset.
The NVM Software Calibration Row, at 0x806020, holds values measured and stored in production test. It is read-only; the application reads each value and writes it into the register it belongs to.
Each device carries a 128-bit serial number spread over four 32-bit words; it is unique only when all four words are used.

Arm Cortex-M0+ revision r0p1, ARMv6-M architecture with the Thumb-2 instruction set, fully instruction compatible with Cortex-M0 and upward compatible with Cortex-M3 and M4. It has two bus interfaces: one 32-bit AMBA-3 AHB-Lite system port to the peripherals and all memory including Flash and RAM, and one 32-bit single-cycle I/O port to the PORT with one-cycle loads and stores.
The core brings the System Control Space (debug registers), the 24-bit SysTick system timer, the NVIC, and the System Control Block for system information, control and system exception handling.

The AHB-Lite bus and the single-cycle I/O port can be used at the same time, so the core fetches its next instructions while it accesses the PORT registers directly, keeping I/O at one cycle per access for as long as needed.

The ARMv6-M NVIC takes 32 external interrupt lines and prioritizes them over 4 priority levels set in software. It is tightly coupled to the core for low latency and quick handling of late-arriving interrupts.
A symmetric crossbar switch with a 32-bit data bus, running at the same clock as the bus masters, that lets different masters reach different slaves at the same time.

Each master reaching the RAM has its own QoS level, which the RAM receives with every access. At level 0x00 or 0x01 an access waits at least one cycle. Concurrent accesses are ordered first by QoS level and then by the static priority of the SRAM port, lowest port ID first. The MTB is fixed at level 3 and the DSU at level 1. The CPU's level is bits [1:0] at address 0x41007110, reset value 0x0; the DMAC's is set in its own QOSCTRL registers.

Each bridge sits on the AHB as a slave and connects the high-speed AHB domain to the low-power APB domain where the peripheral control registers live. It follows AMBA APB v2.0 (APB4) with wait states, error reporting, transaction protection and byte, half-word and word transfers, and in addition merges address and data cycles into one and allows sparse transfers on reads too. It needs CLK_HPBx_AHB running.

Each bridge has one PAC that can write-protect the registers of every peripheral on it. Its APB clock CLK_PACx_APB is controlled in the Power Manager: the PAC clocks of bridges A and B run from reset, while CLK_PAC2_APB starts stopped. The PAC keeps working in any sleep mode whose clock source runs. Debugger accesses ignore the protection. A one written to a peripheral's WPSET bit protects it, and a one in its WPCLR bit unprotects it; both registers read back the same value, so no read-modify-write is needed. A write to a protected peripheral is dropped and raises an access error (CPU exception). Protecting an already protected peripheral, or unprotecting an unprotected one, also raises an error, which can enforce strict protect/unprotect pairing; where interrupts touch protected peripherals, the handler can read WPSET to learn the current state first.

The Device Service Unit detects debugger probes, which lets the Arm Debug Access Port take over the multiplexed debug pads and the CPU reset. It contains a CoreSight Debug ROM for device identification, conforming to the Arm Peripheral Identification specification, and offers memory test services such as those needed for IEC 60730 Class B. Sitting on the bus matrix, it can be used by a debugger and the CPU at once. Some of its features are restricted or absent while the NVMCTRL security bit protects the device. Its features: CPU reset extension, cold- and hot-plug debugger detection, chip erase with status, CRC32 over any memory the bus matrix reaches, CoreSight device identification, two debug communication channels, a security filter on the debug access port, and memory built-in self-test (MBIST).

SWCLK belongs to the DSU by default so it can sense a debugger and stretch the CPU reset. Changing SWCLK's PORT function, or turning off its PORT multiplexing, disables hot-plug detection until a power or external reset. The DSU keeps running in any sleep mode whose clock runs; the Power Manager gates its two bus clocks, CLK_DSU_AHB and CLK_DSU_APB. It has no DMA, interrupt, event or analog connections. Every writable register can be write-protected by the PAC except DCC0 and DCC1; the protection never applies to an external debugger.

If SWCLK is low when RESET is released, the CPU is held in reset after the rest of the system starts, so it runs no code while a debugger connects. SWCLK is pulled up internally at start-up so an unconnected pin is not taken for a debugger. While the CPU is held, STATUSA.CRSTEXT reads one; writing a one releases the CPU and clears the bit, and writing a zero does nothing. On a device protected by the NVMCTRL security bit the CPU cannot be released this way, and the attempt sets STATUSA.PERR.

Cold-plugging is detection while the system is in reset, and is recognised each time a CPU reset extension is triggered. Hot-plugging is detection while the system runs: a falling edge on SWCLK triggers it, as long as SWCLK keeps its default debug function; it cannot occur under reset, since POR and RESET reset the detector. STATUSB.HPE shows whether hot-plugging is available, and STATUSB.DBGPRES is set once either method finds a probe. A protected device offers no hot-plugging. Detection needs the pads powered, so after a cold start it waits for POR release; on a protected device cold-plugging is the only route, the external reset must outlast the POR, and if RESET is released before POR ends the procedure must be repeated until the debugger connects.

Chip-Erase wipes all sensitive content and clears the NVMCTRL security bit: all volatile memories and the whole Flash array, EEPROM emulation area included, are erased, while the auxiliary rows such as the user row stay. It starts when CTRL.CE is written to one, is ignored if the PAC protects the DSU, clears volatile memory before erasing Flash, and signals completion in STATUSA.DONE. On a protected device the debugger must reset the part to be detected. Because the erase relies on clocks and power settings the CPU can change, it is best issued after cold-plugging. Sequence: cold-plug (the probe is detected and the CPU held in reset); write one to CTRL.CE (volatile memories cleared, Flash array erased without the auxiliary rows, lock row erased so the security bit is removed); poll STATUSA.DONE until it reads one; reset the device so NVMCTRL reloads the fuses.

Flash and RAM can be programmed only while the NVMCTRL security bit is clear. A debugger drives RESET low at power-up; the regulator holds the system in POR until the supply passes the POR threshold, then until the internal supplies are safe. The PM starts and switches the core, system, Flash and ungated bus clocks to the slow clock while the external reset keeps internal resets asserted. The debugger holds SWCLK low and releases RESET, which cold-plugs it; it then clocks SWCLK so the DAP runs. Everything but the CPU leaves reset; the CPU stays held. Erasing the chip clears the Flash, and programming proceeds through the AHB-AP. Afterwards the part restarts by asserting RESET, cycling power, or writing one to STATUSA.CRSTEXT; SWCLK must be high when RESET is released, or the CPU will again be held in reset.

Setting the NVMCTRL security bit shuts external tools out of the internal memories; only a Chip-Erase removes it. While protected, AHB-AP reads and writes are confined to the DSU's address range and only some DSU commands work: a security filter watches the AHB-AP transactions and answers any outside the DSU external range with an error that sets the AHB-AP sticky error bits. The CPU uses the DSU without limits even when protected. The first 0x100 bytes of the DSU registers are copied at offset 0x100: 0x00-0xFF is the internal range, 0x100-0x1FF the external range, and a protected device admits MEM-AP accesses only at offsets 0x100-0x2000, under the security restrictions.

A system-level CoreSight ROM table, whose address is in the MEM-AP BASE register of the DAP, identifies the vendor and the identification method. Registers PID0 to PID7 form a 64-bit conceptual ID; PARTNUM 0xCD0 marks the DSU, and REVISION 0x0 means the device is fully identified by DID, which gives processor, family, subfamily and device select.

CRC32 and MBIST share the Address, Length and Data registers: set them up, then write the Control register to start. While a command runs, others are ignored, so STATUSA.DONE must be set before the next one. The DSU is enabled by enabling its clocks. A debug adapter should use the external range 0x100-0x2000; on a protected device the first 0x100 bytes return an error. The CPU has no restriction but should use the internal range 0x0-0x100 to stay clear of the external limits.

The DSU computes a CRC32 over any memory area, Flash and AHB RAM included, with the standard polynomial 0xEDB88320 (reversed form). ADDR takes the word-aligned start and LENGTH the word-aligned size; DATA takes the starting value, normally 0xFFFFFFFF or an earlier result when chaining blocks. Writing one to CTRL.CRC starts it, and CTRL.SWRST aborts it. The result in DATA must be complemented to match common CRC32 code, or used as-is to continue. When done, STATUSA.DONE is set, and STATUSA.BERR must be checked for a bus error. From the external range, and on a protected device, only the whole Flash array or the whole EEPROM emulation area can be checked: ADDR, LENGTH and DATA are forced to fixed values and user values ignored, which still lets a protected device's contents be verified.

DCC0 and DCC1 are two registers with handshake logic that the CPU and debugger can both reach, even on a protected device, at run time or in debug mode, so a custom debug protocol can run over them. On a protected device a debugger cannot connect while the CPU runs, since CRSTEXT cannot be written and the CPU stays in reset. STATUSB.DCC0D and DCC1D flag a new value: set on write, cleared on read. The MBIST logic shares these registers, so they must not be used during MBIST.

MBIST, meant mainly for production test, runs the March LR algorithm, whose run time grows linearly with memory size and depends on CPU clock and bytes tested: write all zeros; per bit, read 0 and write 1 descending; read 1, write 0, read 0, write 1 ascending; read 1, write 0 ascending; read 0, write 1, read 1, write 0 ascending; read all zeros ascending. It finds address decoder, stuck-at, transition, coupling, linked coupling and stuck-open faults. Start: memory start in ADDR.ADDR, size in LENGTH, then one to CTRL.MBIST; CTRL.SWRST aborts. Testing a whole physical memory gives the best coverage. With ADDR.AMOD = 0, the default, the test exits on error: the test ends at the first fault or at success, setting STATUSA.DONE, and STATUSA.FAIL on a fault. With ADDR.AMOD = 1 (pause on error) only STATUSA.FAIL is set at a fault and the test resumes when one is written to it. After a fault, ADDR holds the word with the failing bit and DATA the bit index and phase. MBIST is not available from the external range on a protected device; trying it sets STATUSA.PERR.
An access at DSU offsets 0x200-0x1FFF counts as external; one at offsets 0x0-0x100 counts as internal.

Three blocks make the clocks. SYSCTRL runs the sources: XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M. GCLK holds generic clock generators, each a divider that can take any source, and generic clocks, the per-peripheral clock inputs, each picking a generator through its own multiplexer; separate instances of a peripheral usually get separate generic clocks. Generator 0 is GCLK_MAIN and feeds the PM; generic clock 0 is the DFLL48M reference when the DFLL multiplies another clock. The PM makes the synchronous clocks (CPU, AHB, APB) and masks each peripheral's bus interface clock. Example: SERCOM0 run from the DFLL48M in open loop uses generator 1 on DFLL48M, generic clock 20 (GCLK_SERCOM0_CORE) on generator 1, and CLK_SERCOM0_APB unmasked in the PM's APBC mask.

Synchronous clocks are the CPU and bus clocks; asynchronous clocks are the generic clocks. A peripheral whose core runs on a generic clock has a SYNCBUSY flag that shows a clock-domain crossing in progress. Peripherals with a common synchronizer: ADC, AC, DAC, EIC, GCLK, RTC, TC, WDT. Peripherals with a distributed synchronizer: SERCOM USART, SPI and I2C, I2S, TCC.

Bus-interface registers need no synchronization. Core registers in the generic clock domain are synchronized on every write and some on read, even when both clocks come from one source at one frequency. One synchronizer serves the whole peripheral, so one register is in flight at a time. A write sets STATUS.SYNCBUSY until done; meanwhile another core write, a read of a read-synchronized register or a read of the register being written stalls the bus, while other core registers and APB registers read without a stall. A read-synchronized read stalls at once without setting SYNCBUSY, and stalls twice if a write is still pending. Completion is seen by polling SYNCBUSY, by the synchronization-ready interrupt where one exists, or by simply issuing the next access, which waits.

Where a READREQ register exists, writing RREQ with ADDR (the register's offset from the peripheral base) synchronizes that register once, setting SYNCBUSY until done; its value then reads without delay until RREQ is written again. RCONT keeps the register synchronized continuously so the latest value always reads without stalling; SYNCBUSY is set only for the first pass. A write to a write-synchronized register stops a continuous request, which must then be restarted, and continuous requests pause in sleep modes that stop the generic clock.

Writing CTRL.ENABLE starts a synchronization and sets SYNCBUSY; the bit reads back its new value at once. Writing CTRL.SWRST does the same; it reads as one at once and hardware clears it, with SYNCBUSY, when the reset is done; writing zero to it does nothing. During either, a core or APB register write or a read-synchronized read stalls the bus; APB reads do not. The synchronization-ready interrupt does not report either of these.

Each write-synchronized core register has its own synchronizer and its own SYNCBUSY bit, so different registers can be written back to back; a second write to the same register before its synchronization ends is dropped. With 8-bit REGA and REGB and a 16-bit REGC, REGA then REGB at once is fine and a 16-bit REGC write is fine, but REGC written as two 8-bit writes loses the second write and flags an error; a 32-bit write over all three updates them at different moments. Reads return immediately but are valid only when the register's SYNCBUSY bit is clear. Writing CTRL.ENABLE sets SYNCBUSY.ENABLE and writing CTRL.SWRST sets SYNCBUSY.SWRST; neither is reported by the synchronization-ready interrupt.

A peripheral on a generic clock needs a running clock source, an enabled generic clock generator set to that source, its generic clock enabled and pointed at that generator, and its bus interface unmasked in the PM. While masked, its registers read as zero and writes are lost.

Every clock source can run on demand: it stops while nothing requests it and starts when a request arrives from a peripheral, through its generic clock and generator, all of which must be enabled for the request to pass. Clearing a source's ONDEMAND bit keeps it always running, removing the start-up wait at the cost of power. Requests still work in standby for modules set to run in standby (RUNSTDBY). A slow peripheral clock lowers active power but lengthens every synchronization with the CPU domain.

Any reset: OSC8M on and divided by 8, GCLK_MAIN on OSC8M, CPU and bus clocks undivided. Power reset: every generator off except generator 0 (GCLK_MAIN) on OSC8M undivided and generator 2 on OSCULP32K undivided, and every generic clock off except the WDT's, on generator 2. A user reset restores the same, except write-locked generic clocks (WRTLOCK set, or the WDT clock when the NVM User Row sets WDT always-on at power-up) and the RTC generic clock if enabled. Clock sources return to reset state on any reset, except the 32 kHz sources, which only a power reset resets.

The generic clock controller has eight generic clock generators feeding m generic clock multiplexers, m set by the peripheral count. A generator takes an internal or external source (including a GCLK_IO pin), optionally divides it, and can change source on the fly; each multiplexer picks a generator and gates it into one peripheral clock, GCLK_PERIPHERAL. One generic clock can clock several peripherals. GCLK works in every sleep mode; its bus clock CLK_GCLK_APB is set in the PM's APBAMASK. It has no DMA, interrupt or event lines, and its writable registers can be PAC-protected.

Enable the generator's source first. Then: one 32-bit write to GENDIV with the generator in ID and the divider in DIV; one 32-bit write to GENCTRL with the generator in ID and GENEN set; one 16-bit write to CLKCTRL with the generic clock in ID and the generator in GEN. GCLK has no module enable bit. CTRL.SWRST returns every register to reset except locked generic clocks and their generators.

Each generator chooses among eight sources, GCLKGEN[1] among seven since it cannot feed itself; GCLKGEN[1] can feed every other generator. Generator x pairs with pin GCLK_IO[x], which can be its source or carry its output. The chosen source can be divided, and each generator is enabled on its own with GENCTRL.GENEN; when GENEN reads zero its output is gated off. GCLKGEN[0] is GCLK_MAIN, the PM's main clock. Changing GENCTRL.SRC from source A to B is glitch-free: the generator keeps running on A until B is ready, holding requests to both, then releases A.

GENDIV.DIV divides the source; GENCTRL.DIVSEL sets which of two ways the integer divider reads DIV, and the width of DIV differs between generators. An odd divisor gives an uneven duty cycle unless GENCTRL.IDC is set, which makes it 50/50.

With GENCTRL.OE and GENEN set, the generator requests its source and drives its clock onto GCLK_IO. With OE clear the pin holds the GENCTRL.OOV level, which is also the level when the generator is off. In standby an output clock freezes at OOV unless GENCTRL.RUNSTDBY is set, which keeps it running on the pin.

operation.topic: Generic clock enable and source change
operation.text: A generic clock is given a generator in CLKCTRL.GEN and turned on with CLKCTRL.CLKEN; CLKEN crosses into the generic clock domain and reads its old value until synchronized. Writing CLKEN to zero gates the clock off. To change GEN without glitches: clear CLKEN, wait for it to read zero, write GEN, set CLKEN.

Setting CLKCTRL.WRTLOCK locks that generic clock's CLKCTRL against further writes, and also locks the GENCTRL and GENDIV of the generator feeding it. Only a power reset unlocks them; SWRST does not. GCLKGEN[0] cannot be locked, since it is GCLK_MAIN and every reset restarts it in a known state.

GENCTRL, GENDIV and CLKCTRL are reached indirectly through their ID fields: a write carries the ID of the generator or generic clock it configures. To read one, first write its ID (an 8-bit write to GENCTRL.ID, for example), then read the register. Reset values of these registers differ per generator and per generic clock.

GCLK supports SleepWalking: in a sleep mode that stops generic clocks, a peripheral that needs its clock requests it, and GCLK wakes the source, then the generator, then the generic clock, and delivers it. In standby a generator can keep driving its GCLK_IO pin.

GENCTRL, GENDIV and CTRL are synchronized on write. STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done; an access that needs synchronization while it is set stalls the bus, holding the CPU and leaving interrupts pending until it completes.

The power manager handles reset, synchronous clock generation and sleep modes. Reset sources: power resets POR, BOD12 and BOD33; user resets from the RESET pin, the watchdog and software; the cause is read from a status register. Clocks: CPU, AHB and APB clocks from GCLK_MAIN through a prescaler dividing by 1 to 128, safe switching at run time, per-module clock masks and a clock failure detector that can fall back to OSC8M. Sleep modes are IDLE and STANDBY, with SleepWalking on GCLK clocks. In STANDBY the regulator runs in low-power mode, so enough clocks and peripherals must be off beforehand that it is not overloaded.

CLK_PM_APB can be masked in the PM, but once off only a reset turns it back on. GCLK_MAIN, set up by GCLK, is the main clock (CLK_MAIN), which feeds one 8-bit prescaler for all synchronous clocks. CLK_CPU drives the CPU; stopping it halts execution. CLK_AHB matches the CPU clock in phase and frequency but can run while the CPU clock is off, and each AHB peripheral clock is gated from it. Each APBx clock is synchronous to the CPU, may be divided, runs with the CPU clock off, and gates each module's APB clock.

The PM interrupt sources are Clock Ready and Clock Failure Detector, on one line to the NVIC; INTFLAG shows which. While debugging, the PM keeps its clocks running in sleep so the debugger can reach every module, so power cannot be measured in debug mode. All writable registers except INTFLAG and RCAUSE can be PAC-protected. The PM is always on and cannot be reset; in IDLE modes it runs on the main clock and in STANDBY it is frozen until an asynchronous interrupt.

After power-on the PM is running, RCAUSE shows POR, the default GCLK_MAIN source is started and calibrated before the CPU runs, the main clock is GCLK_MAIN with no prescaling, and the device is in ACTIVE mode with only the needed clocks on.

CPUSEL.CPUDIV divides the main clock for the CPU (and AHB); APBxSEL.APBxDIV divides it for each APB bus. f_CPU must be at least f_APBx, and no domain may exceed its maximum frequency. CPUSEL and APBxSEL can be written without stopping any peripheral; one write updates all synchronous clocks together, and any can be left unchanged, for example to scale the CPU while the APB stays fixed.

After CPUSEL or APBxSEL is written, INTFLAG.CKRDY reads zero until the new setting takes effect, and can raise the PM interrupt when it does. Rewriting CPUSEL before CKRDY is back at one can leave the system unstable or hung.

Each AHB and APBx peripheral clock has a bit in the AHBMASK or APBxMASK register; a module on several domains has several bits. A module without its APB clock cannot be read or written until its bit is set again. Masking NVMCTRL breaks flash reads by the CPU; masking the PM or its APB bridge leaves the masks unwritable until a system reset.

When CTRL.CFDEN is set, the detector watches the undivided main clock for at least one rising edge in each OSCULP32K period. If none comes, the main clock moves to OSC8M, INTFLAG.CFD is set (with an interrupt if enabled) and CTRL.BKUPCLK reads one; writing BKUPCLK to zero returns to GCLK_MAIN without curing the fault. The detector does not watch during start-up after wake-up or in sleep, and must be off before standby. It must not be used when the main clock is not much faster than OSCULP32K (for instance a 32 kHz RC main clock), and OSC8M should be enabled so the switch can happen.

RCAUSE holds the cause of the latest reset for the boot code. Power resets come from electrical events (POR, BOD12, BOD33, all generated in SYSCTRL); user resets come from the application: the RESET pin pulled low, the watchdog, or SysResetReq from the CPU's SYSRESETREQ bit. RESET has an internal pull-up and needs no drive in normal use. The power-on reset detector holds the device in reset until power is stable, so no external reset circuit is needed for a clean power-up.

WFI enters sleep; SLEEP.IDLE and the CPU's SCR.SLEEPDEEP pick the mode. IDLE stops the CPU and, by IDLE level, the AHB and APB clock domains, regardless of the PM mask bits; the regulator stays in normal mode. Enter it with SLEEPDEEP zero, or automatically on leaving the lowest-priority ISR if SCR.SLEEPONEXIT is set; any interrupt unmasked in the NVIC with enough priority wakes it to ACTIVE. STANDBY (SLEEPDEEP one) stops every clock except those a running module requests or whose ONDEMAND is zero, puts regulator and RAM in low-power mode, also supports SLEEPONEXIT, and wakes on any asynchronous interrupt, after which the ISR runs or execution simply continues as PRIMASK decides. The RTC, for example, can run in standby with its generic clock source on.

SleepWalking lets a peripheral briefly wake its clocks in STANDBY to do a task without waking the CPU; afterwards the device either wakes on that peripheral's interrupt or returns to STANDBY. On this device it works only on GCLK clocks, through on-demand clock sources.

SYSCTRL is the interface to the clock sources, the brown-out detectors, the core regulator and the voltage reference: enable, disable, calibrate and monitor. All their status bits gather in PCLKSR and can raise interrupts; BOD33 and BOD12 interrupts can wake the device from standby. Sources: XOSC 0.4-32 MHz crystal oscillator (tunable gain, programmable start-up, crystal or external clock on XIN); XOSC32K 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator (automatic or manual gain, programmable start-up, crystal or external clock on XIN32); OSC32K 32.768 kHz high-accuracy RC (fine tuning, programmable start-up); OSCULP32K 32.768 kHz ultra-low-power always-on RC (fine tuning, factory calibration loaded at reset); OSC8M 8 MHz RC (fast start-up, fine tuning, 4/2/1 MHz divided outputs, factory calibration loaded at reset); DFLL48M 48 MHz, no external parts, open loop or locked to a reference; FDPLL96M 48 to 96 MHz output from a 32 kHz to 2 MHz reference, three reference choices, adjustable PI controller, 1/16 reference-step fractional part.

BOD33 (3.3 V) and BOD12 (1.2 V): programmable threshold loaded from the Flash user calibration at start-up, reset or interrupt action, continuous or sampled mode with programmable rate, hysteresis. VREF: bandgap with programmable calibration (factory value loaded at start-up) and a temperature sensor. VREG: trimmable core voltage, trim loaded from factory calibration at start-up.

SYSCTRL provides XOSC, XOSC32K, OSC32K, OSCULP32K, OSC8M, DFLL48M and FDPLL96M to GCLK, and keeps working in any sleep mode where its clock runs. CLK_SYSCTRL_APB is set in the PM. The BOD sampling clock and the DFLL48M control logic run asynchronously to the bus, so some writes need synchronization. The FDPLL96M reference comes from XOSC32K, XOSC (through a divider) or a generic clock, and must be set up and running first, within the FDPLL96M input range; its internal lock timer needs a 32 kHz generic clock. In debug halt SYSCTRL keeps running; if debugger cold-plugging is detected the BOD33 reset is masked, while under hot-plugging it stays active. INTFLAG is the one writable register without PAC protection.

A 32.768 kHz crystal goes between XIN32 and XOUT32 and a 0.4-32 MHz crystal between XIN and XOUT, each with the load capacitors it needs; the electrical characteristics give crystal and capacitor values.

Each oscillator is turned on and off with the ENABLE bit of its control register. By default (ONDEMAND = 1, RUNSTDBY = 0) an oscillator runs in idle only when a peripheral requests it and stops in standby. ONDEMAND = 0 makes it run always in idle. RUNSTDBY = 1 lets it run in standby on request (not for DFLL48M and FDPLL96M); ONDEMAND = 0 with RUNSTDBY = 1 keeps it running in standby. OSCULP32K always runs and cannot be disabled.

XOSC takes either an external clock on XIN or a 0.4-32 MHz crystal. It is off at reset, leaving XIN/XOUT as GPIO. With XOSC.XTALEN set (crystal) SYSCTRL takes both pins; with XTALEN clear (external clock) it takes only XIN and XOUT stays GPIO. In crystal mode XOSC.GAIN must match the crystal frequency; XOSC.AMPGC adjusts amplitude automatically and in most cases lowers current. After reset or wake-up the output is masked for the start-up time set by XOSC.STARTUP, after which PCLKSR.XOSCRDY sets and can interrupt. Standby must not be entered while any oscillator is still starting: wait for its ready bit.

XOSC32K takes an external clock on XIN32 or a 32.768 kHz crystal between XIN32 and XOUT32; pin use follows XOSC32K.XTALEN as for XOSC. It is off after POR. Turn it off by clearing only ENABLE; writing ENABLE together with other bits may behave unpredictably. Once on it stays on in every sleep mode. Start-up is set by XOSC32K.STARTUP, with the output masked until PCLKSR.XOSC32KRDY sets. Because a crystal can need up to one second to start, XOSC32K keeps running through every reset except POR. With a crystal it offers a 32.768 kHz output (EN32K) and a 1.024 kHz output (EN1K); neither is available with an external clock on XIN32.

OSC32K is a tunable low-power 32 kHz RC oscillator, off by default and turned on with OSC32K.ENABLE. EN32K enables its 32.768 kHz output and EN1K its 1.024 kHz output. Its frequency is set by OSC32K.CALIB, which software must load from the factory values in the NVM software calibration row; a new CALIB takes effect once PCLKSR.OSC32KRDY goes high.

OSCULP32K is the ultra-low-power 32 kHz RC oscillator, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature, preferred over OSC32K when power matters more than accuracy. It is on after POR and runs always except during POR; its 32.768 kHz and 1.024 kHz outputs never stop. OSCULP32K.CALIB is loaded from factory calibration at start-up to correct for process spread and can be overwritten.

OSC8M is an open-loop 8 MHz RC oscillator, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature, so its frequency moves with voltage, temperature and process. It is the clock after POR and the backup clock for a main-clock failure. OSC8M.ENABLE turns it on and off. CALIB is loaded from factory calibration at start-up; FRANGE and CALIB can be rewritten; doing so while it is enabled is not recommended. It stops on its own in some sleep modes.

Every reset selects open loop, where DFLLVAL.COARSE and DFLLVAL.FINE set the output frequency; loading the DFLL48M COARSE CAL calibration value into COARSE gives close to 48 MHz. COARSE and FINE can be changed while the DFLL48M runs. CLK_DFLL48M is usable once PCLKSR.DFLLRDY sets.

In closed loop the output is regulated against a reference, generic clock 0 (CLK_DFLL48M_REF). After enabling the DFLL48M: enable and select the reference; set the largest coarse and fine steps in DFLLMUL.CSTEP and FSTEP (no more than half the maximum of COARSE and FINE; small steps mean little overshoot but slower lock); set DFLLMUL.MUL so the output stays below the DFLL maximum (a target below the minimum gives the minimum); then set DFLLCTRL.MODE. COARSE and FINE become read-only and are driven by the tuner, which starts from the existing COARSE value. Loading DFLL48M COARSE CAL into COARSE, setting DFLLCTRL.BPLCKC, then closing the loop cuts the lock time to the fine-lock time.

Locking runs in two stages: coarse lock finds COARSE and sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKC; fine lock trims FINE and sets PCLKSR.DFLLLOCKF; each can interrupt. The clock is usable when DFLLRDY sets, with accuracy depending on which locks are set. In closed loop the ratio between output and reference is measured all the time and its difference from MUL is kept in DFLLVAL.DIFF.

With DFLLCTRL.STABLE zero the tuner follows drift without losing lock, so FINE may change after every measurement. An unstable or drifting reference can push FINE past its limits, setting PCLKSR.DFLLOOB; the closed-loop reference has to be steady: an external oscillator is advised, an internal one is not allowed, and XOSC32K is the best choice. If the reference stops or falls below CLK_DFLL48M/(2 × MUL_MAX), PCLKSR.DFLLRCS sets after up to about 2^17 output cycles; the DFLL48M then acts as in open loop and resumes closed loop when the reference returns.

operation.topic: DFLL48M chill cycle and quick lock
operation.text: A new output frequency can take several microseconds to appear, which with a small MUL can upset locking. A chill cycle, on by default and turned off with DFLLCTRL.CCDIS, skips measurement after each change and may double the lock time. Quick Lock, also on by default and turned off with DFLLCTRL.QLDIS, relaxes the lock condition; the output spreads more than with chill cycles but averages the same.

With DFLLCTRL.LLAW zero, a DFLL48M turned off and on again restarts with its old settings and keeps its locks, even without a reference, and fine tracking corrects drift once the reference is back (if STABLE is zero). With LLAW one it loses all locks when turned off and relocks from the start. Accuracy at fine lock depends on the fine step size (smaller at higher output frequency), the measurement resolution (a small output-to-reference ratio can lock low, so a reference of 32 kHz or less is recommended for low targets) and the reference's own accuracy.

The FDPLL96M is a fractional digital PLL: time-to-digital converter, PI digital filter, digitally controlled oscillator and ÷N feedback. The reference CLK_FDPLL96M_REF is CLK_DPLL_REF0 (XOSC32K), CLK_DPLL_REF1 (XOSC through a divider) or GCLK_DPLL; the output is CK_GATED, released by its final clock gate. The lock timer needs GCLK_DPLL_32K. With DPLLRATIO.LDRFRAC zero it runs in integer mode; otherwise fractional mode, which adds jitter. Disabling it resets the output.

DPLLCTRLA.ENABLE turns it on and off. The output is stable once DPLLSTATUS.LOCK is set. With DPLLCTRLB.LTIME non-zero a fixed user lock time validates lock; with LTIME zero lock follows the PLL's own status and its time varies with filter and target frequency. DPLLCTRLB.WUF (wake-up fast) opens the output gate at the end of start-up, before the frequency has settled, saving several milliseconds. After first acquisition, DPLLCTRLB.LBYPASS decides whether loss of lock gates the output off.

operation.topic: FDPLL96M reference switching and ratio changes
operation.text: To change reference: disable the FDPLL96M, change DPLLCTRLB.REFCLK, enable again. DPLLRATIO may be rewritten while running; LOCK clears and sets again when the output settles, and the lock-fail flag INTFLAG.DPLLLCK sets on the falling edge of lock until cleared by writing one. The PI filter adjusts itself, but DPLLCTRLB.FILTER can override it, and DPLLCTRLB.LPEN bypasses the TDC.

BOD33 watches VDDANA and BOD12 watches VDDCORE. Threshold (BOD33.LEVEL), action (reset or interrupt), hysteresis and enable load from the Flash user row at start-up and POR and can be overwritten. Crossing below the threshold gives a reset or an interrupt, and PCLKSR.BOD33DET shows the state. Continuous mode (MODE = 0) is the default for both; BOD12 has no continuous mode in standby. Sampling mode (MODE = 1) powers the detector briefly at each tick of a clock derived from OSCULP32K's 1 kHz output, divided by PSEL. Writes to BOD33 or BOD12 are ignored while PCLKSR.B33SRDY or B12SRDY is zero; clear CEN before changing PSEL, wait for the ready bit, then write PSEL. HYST adds hysteresis in either mode.

VREG supplies VDDCORE. It is on after every reset and can be turned off with VREG.ENABLE. VREG.LEVEL is loaded from factory calibration at reset. VREG.VDDMON monitors the core supply and applies a power-on reset if it falls below a critical level, well under the BOD12 threshold; code restarts only once the supply is back.

VREF is a bandgap reference, factory-calibrated at typical voltage and temperature with VREF.CAL loaded at reset, plus a temperature sensor with a linear output voltage over C_MIN to C_MAX. VREF.TSEN turns the sensor on; it can be routed to the ADC, and VREF.BGOUTEN routes the bandgap output to the ADC as well. VREF.CALIB sets the bandgap level and can be overwritten.

Sources, each on a 0-to-1 change of its PCLKSR bit: XOSCRDY, XOSC32KRDY, OSC32KRDY, OSC8MRDY, DFLLRDY, DFLLOOB, DFLLLOCKF, DFLLLOCKC, DFLLRCS, BOD33RDY, BOD33DET, B33SRDY, BOD12RDY, BOD12DET, B12SRDY; and from the PLL, LOCK, LOCKL (falling edge of lock in normal operation) and LTTO (the DPLLCTRLB.LTIME time has passed since start). All share one NVIC line; INTFLAG shows which.

Check PCLKSR.DFLLRDY before writing any DFLL48M control register; writes while it is zero are ignored. To read a DFLL48M register, write DFLLSYNC.READREQ and read once DFLLRDY is set; reading without it starts a synchronization and halts the bus until done, except when the DFLL48M is off. The BOD prescaler counters are also asynchronous: writing BOD33 or BOD12 clears B33SRDY or B12SRDY until done, and meanwhile another write, or a read of the register written, stalls the bus.

The watchdog resets the system unless cleared within its time-out period, recovering from runaway or deadlocked code. Window mode adds a closed period before the open one: a clear too early or too late resets. An early-warning interrupt can come before time-out. It runs in active and all sleep modes from a clock independent of the CPU, and still resets or interrupts if the main clocks fail. Time-out runs from 8 to 16,000 cycles in normal mode and 16 to 32,000 in window mode, and it has an always-on option.

CLK_WDT_APB is on by default. GCLK_WDT clocks the counter and is meant to come from the ultra-low-power 32 kHz oscillator, whose loose accuracy makes the real time-out vary between devices; a more accurate source costs more power. WDT interrupts can wake the device; in debug halt the WDT stops unless forced to run. INTFLAG is not PAC-protected.

CTRL (except ENABLE), CONFIG and EWCTRL, and the bits CTRL.WEN and CTRL.ALWAYSON, are writable only while the WDT is off; writes while it is on or turning on are dropped. Normal mode needs CONFIG.PER; early warning adds EWCTRL.EWOFFSET and INTENSET.EW; window mode adds CONFIG.WINDOW and CTRL.WEN. At power-on CTRL.ENABLE, ALWAYSON, WEN, CONFIG.WINDOW, CONFIG.PER and EWCTRL.EWOFFSET load from the NVM User Row. CTRL.ENABLE turns it on and off, but it cannot be turned off while ALWAYSON is set.

CONFIG.PER selects one of 12 time-out periods, 8 ms to 16 s; writing 0xA5 to CLEAR is accepted anywhere inside it and starts a new period. Writing any other value to CLEAR resets the system at once. The early-warning interrupt, off by default, fires EWCTRL.EWOFFSET GCLK_WDT cycles after the period starts: with PER = 0x2 and EWOFFSET = 0x1 it fires at 16 cycles and the reset comes at 32. An offset longer than the period means the reset comes first and the warning never does.

The closed period (CONFIG.WINDOW, 8 ms to 16 s) comes first, and a clear inside it resets the system; the open period (CONFIG.PER, 8 ms to 16 s) follows, and the clear must fall there. The total time-out is the sum. The early-warning interrupt fires at the start of the open period, which lets a sleeping system wake, clear the watchdog and carry on.

Setting CTRL.ALWAYSON keeps the WDT running whatever CTRL.ENABLE says, and only a power-on reset clears it. CONFIG and EWCTRL become read-only, so PER, WINDOW and EWOFFSET are fixed; window mode can still be switched with CTRL.WEN and the early-warning interrupt enabled or disabled.

The one interrupt source is Early Warning, on a single line. CTRL and CLEAR are synchronized on write; STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done, INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal the end, and an access needing synchronization while busy stalls the bus.

A 32-bit counter behind a 10-bit prescaler, normally running all the time. Modes: 32-bit counter with one 32-bit compare or two 16-bit compares in 16-bit mode, and clock/calendar (seconds, minutes, hours in 12 or 24 h, day, month, year, leap-year correction). It wakes the device from sleep by alarm or compare, periodic or overflow, gives periodic events from the prescaler, can clear on a match, and has digital frequency correction. Usual clock: the 1.024 kHz output of OSC32K, lowest power; the 32.768 kHz output gives better than 1 ms resolution; other sources come through GCLK. From 32.768 kHz the smallest tick is 30.5 µs and time-outs reach 36 hours; with a 1 s tick the longest time-out is over 136 years.

The RTC runs in any sleep mode and its interrupts can wake the device. Only POR or CTRL.SWRST resets it. GCLK_RTC must be set up in GCLK first and must never come from generic clock generator 0. A 32.768 kHz crystal on XIN32 and XOUT32 can be its source. In debug halt it stops unless DBGCTRL lets it run. INTFLAG, READREQ, STATUS and DBGCTRL are not PAC-protected.

CTRL.MODE, CTRL.PRESCALER, CTRL.MATCHCLR, CTRL.CLKREP and EVCTRL are writable only while the RTC is off. Before enabling, set the mode, the clock representation and the prescaler. CTRL.ENABLE turns it on and off; disable it before a CTRL.SWRST, which resets everything except DBGCTRL and leaves it off.

Mode 0: COUNT increments on each rising edge of CLK_RTC_CNT up to 0xFFFFFFFF, then wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. It is compared with COMP0; a match sets INTFLAG.CMP0 on the next counter clock edge. With CTRL.MATCHCLR set the counter clears on the cycle after a match, giving periodic interrupts longer than prescaler events, and CMP0 and OVF set together.
Mode 1: COUNT counts up to the 16-bit PER value, then wraps to 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. It is compared with COMP0 and COMP1; a match sets INTFLAG.CMPn on the next counter clock edge.

Mode 2: the counter must be clocked at 1 Hz. CLOCK holds seconds, minutes, hours (12 or 24 h by CTRL.CLKREP, changeable only while off), day of month from 1, month from 1 and a year offset from a software-defined reference. Every year divisible by 4 is treated as a leap year, so the reference must be a leap year such as 2000. After 23:59:59 on 31 December of year 63 it wraps to 00:00:00 on 1 January of year 0 and sets INTFLAG.OVF. CLOCK is compared with ALARM0 through the field mask in MASK0.SEL; a match sets INTFLAG.ALARM0 on the next counter edge, one second late at 1 Hz. MATCHCLR clears the clock after an alarm match, setting ALARM0 and OVF together.

Any of prescaler bits 2 to 9 can make an event, chosen with EVCTRL.PEREOn, on that bit's rising edge. They run independently of the counter's prescaler setting, except that none are made when CTRL.PRESCALER is zero.

Correction needs CTRL.PRESCALER greater than 1. Once every 1024 GCLK_RTC cycles the prescaler may gain or skip one count; FREQCORR.VALUE sets how many of 976 such periods are corrected, in steps of about 1 ppm, and FREQCORR.SIGN sets faster (positive) or slower (negative). The correction also shifts the spacing of periodic events around the end of each correction cycle.

Interrupt sources: Overflow, Compare n, Alarm n and Synchronization Ready, on one line. Output events: OVF, PERn, CMPn and ALARMn, each enabled by its EVCTRL bit. RTC interrupts wake the device; without an enabled interrupt the CPU wakes and continues after the sleep instruction. Periodic events can wake the CPU through an event channel with its interrupt on. Waking from a shutdown mode, RTC registers keep their values except INTENCLR/SET, READREQ, INTFLAG and DBGCTRL (interrupts come back disabled), STATUS shows what happened, and the CPU starts from the reset address.

CTRL.SWRST, CTRL.ENABLE, COUNT, CLOCK, PER, COMPn, ALARMn, FREQCORR and MASKn are synchronized on write; COUNT and CLOCK on read too. STATUS.SYNCBUSY sets at once and clears when done, INTFLAG.SYNCRDY can signal the end, and an access needing synchronization while busy stalls the bus.

The DMAC holds a DMA engine and a CRC engine. Channels raise transfer requests on their triggers; an arbiter grants one active channel at a time; the fetch engine loads the channel's descriptor from SRAM; a higher-priority channel can interrupt, after the active channel's descriptor is written back to SRAM. Four bus interfaces: an AHB master for data, an APB slave for registers, an AHB master for descriptor fetch and an AHB master for write-back.

Peripheral-to-peripheral, peripheral-to-memory, memory-to-peripheral and memory-to-memory transfers, triggered by software, events or peripheral requests. Descriptors in SRAM, single or linked for multi-buffer and circular use. 6 channels with automatic descriptor fetch and suspend/resume; 4 priority levels per channel, fixed or round-robin within a level. 1 to 256 kB in one block; static or incrementing addresses. Interrupts on block complete, error and suspend. 4 event inputs and 4 event outputs, one each on channels 0 to 3; inputs can start normal, periodic or conditional transfers or suspend/resume, outputs fire on beat, burst, block or transaction. Write-back section per channel for error handling. CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) or CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3).

CLK_DMAC_APB and the AHB clock CLK_DMAC_AHB are set in the PM; the APB clock is synchronous to the AHB clock, may be divided and can run with the AHB clock off. The DMAC runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs and its interrupts can wake the device. In debug halt it stops unless DBGCTRL lets it run. INTPEND, CHID and CHINTFLAG are not PAC-protected.

A beat is one bus access, sized by BTCTRL.BEATSIZE. A burst is n beats, with n = 1 on this device, and cannot be interrupted. A block is what one descriptor moves, 1 to 64k beats, and can be interrupted between bursts. A transaction is all blocks in a linked list. A trigger (software, event or peripheral) makes the channel request the arbiter; the granted channel runs its descriptor and can be pre-empted after each burst. Optional event per beat; optional interrupts and event per block. At the end of a transaction the channel is suspended or disabled as configured.

BASEADDR and WRBADDR are writable only with the DMAC off; CTRL.SWRST only with both DMAC and CRC off; CHCTRLB (except CMD and LVL) and CHCTRLA.SWRST only with that channel off; CRCCTRL and CRCCHKSUM only with the CRC off. Before enabling: write BASEADDR and WRBADDR, enable the priority levels in CTRL.LVLENx. Per channel: select it in CHID, set CHCTRLB.TRIGACT and TRIGSRC; in its first descriptor set BEATSIZE, VALID, BTCNT, SRCADDR and DSTADDR. For CRC set CRCCTRL.CRCSRC, CRCPOLY and, for I/O input, CRCBEATSIZE.

CTRL.DMAENABLE turns the DMAC on and off; CHCTRLA.ENABLE turns on the channel selected in CHID; CTRL.CRCENABLE the CRC. CTRL.SWRST, with DMAC and CRC off, resets everything except DBGCTRL. CHCTRLA.SWRST resets the selected channel, which must be off.

A channel needs a valid first descriptor before it is enabled and triggered. All descriptors live in SRAM. BASEADDR points to the first descriptor of channel 0, and the first descriptors of all channels sit next to each other in channel order. WRBADDR points to the write-back section, where the DMAC keeps each channel's ongoing descriptor, also in channel order. Using the low channels saves memory. The two sections may be separate, so a channel's transaction can be repeated without rewriting its first descriptor, or shared (BASEADDR = WRBADDR), which uses less SRAM and shortens the delay from fetching the first descriptor to the first burst.

An enabled, unsuspended channel that sees a trigger joins the pending queue and sets PENDCH.PENDCHx; when granted, PENDCHx clears and BUSYCH.BUSYCHx sets. After its burst the channel requeues (BUSYCHx stays set), waits for a trigger, suspends or is disabled (BUSYCHx clears). A suspended channel leaves the queue but keeps PENDCHx; a disabled one leaves and clears it. ACTIVE.LVLEXx shows a level pending or transferring. Levels are enabled with CTRL.LVLENx; with all enabled a lower level number wins. Within a level PRICTRL0.RRLVLENx = 0 gives static priority to the lowest channel number, which can starve high channels; RRLVLENx = 1 gives round-robin, the last granted channel dropping to lowest, its number kept in PRICTRL0.LVLPRIx.

The granted channel's descriptor is fetched from the descriptor section (new block) or the write-back section (ongoing block). Arbitration runs after every burst; BTCNT drops by the beats moved, and if another channel takes over, the remaining count is saved to write-back before that channel's descriptor is loaded. When BTCNT reaches zero, VALID is cleared and the descriptor is written back; transfer-complete and suspend interrupts and the block event fire if enabled. If DESCADDR is 0x00000000 the transaction ends and the channel suspends or disables per BTCTRL.BLOCKACT; otherwise the next descriptor is fetched and copied into the channel's write-back slot ahead of the next arbitration.

Each channel picks its trigger in CHCTRLB.TRIGSRC and what it starts in CHCTRLB.TRIGACT: a block by default, or a beat or a whole transaction. A single descriptor disables the channel after its block; a list disables it after the last descriptor, or waits for the next trigger while descriptors remain. One extra trigger during a transfer is kept pending (CHSTATUS.PEND, PENDCH); further ones are lost. CHSTATUS.BUSY and BUSYCH show a transfer in progress.

Source and destination can each be fixed or incrementing. BTCTRL.SRCINC turns on source increment; with BTCTRL.STEPSEL one the source steps by STEPSIZE, otherwise by one beat. BTCTRL.DSTINC turns on destination increment; with STEPSEL zero the destination steps by STEPSIZE, otherwise by one beat. With increment on, SRCADDR or DSTADDR holds the address of the block's last beat, not its first.

An AHB bus error disables the active channel and sets CHINTFLAG.TERR (interrupt optional); BTCNT is not decremented and is written back first. Fetching an invalid descriptor (VALID zero), or resuming into a next address of 0x00000000, suspends the channel and sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP and CHSTATUS.FERR.

Each descriptor's DESCADDR points to the next; DESCADDR = 0x00000000 marks the last. To append, build the new descriptor with a zero DESCADDR and point the old last one at it. To change a descriptor in a running list: enable the suspend interrupt before enabling the channel, prepare the new descriptor, clear VALID on the one being changed, read DESCADDR from write-back; if the DMA has not reached it, update and set VALID again (optionally resume); if it is executing it, suspend the channel, update the write-back DESCADDR, clear flags and resume, then update and revalidate. To insert C between A and B: impossible while B runs; if A has not started, clear A's VALID, point A at C and C at B, set A's VALID; if A is running, suspend first, do the same, then resume.

Software suspends a channel with CHCTRLB.CMD; it stops after the current burst and the command clears itself. BTCTRL.BLOCKACT can suspend after a block: the channel stays enabled and keeps receiving triggers but leaves arbitration. An invalid descriptor also suspends it, setting CHSTATUS.FERR. Only an enabled channel can be suspended; disabling it clears a pending suspend. Suspension sets CHINTFLAG.SUSP. The Resume command restarts a suspended channel where it stopped, and issued before a suspend it makes the next suspend be skipped.

Channels with event inputs act on CHCTRLB.EVACT once CHCTRLB.EVIE is set; only resynchronized events are supported. Normal transfer: the event triggers a beat or burst, with TRIGSRC zero; an event arriving while pending is lost. Periodic transfer: the event lets a pending peripheral trigger through, for timed protocols. Conditional transfer: each peripheral trigger is stored when the event arrives, for peripheral-to-peripheral chains. Conditional block: a block starts only after an event, which is acknowledged when the block ends. Suspend: the event suspends after the current AHB access. Resume: the event resumes and clears CHINTFLAG.SUSP. Skip next block suspend: resumes a suspended channel, or is held until the next block suspend, which it cancels.

Channels with event outputs pulse for one AHB clock cycle. CHCTRLB.EVOE enables the output and each descriptor's BTCTRL.EVOSEL picks beat, burst or block; for an event at transaction end, select the block event in the last descriptor only.

Disabling a channel aborts its transfer cleanly; disabling the DMAC aborts everything. On a DMAC disable the active channel stops after its current beat and write-back, and the others stop on the next clock. CHCTRLA.ENABLE and CTRL.DMAENABLE read zero once the channel or module is actually off.

CRC-16 (CRC-CCITT) is the default polynomial and CRC-32 (IEEE 802.3) the other choice. A CRC-n catches any single burst of up to n bits and all but 2^-n of longer bursts. Input comes from a DMA channel or from the APB interface; the result is in CRCCHKSUM, bit-reversed and complemented for CRC-32. The engine works a byte at a time. On a DMA channel it uses the channel's beat size and the checksum is ready when the transaction completes or aborts; SRAM, Flash or I/O data can be checked by sending it through a channel to CRCDATAIN. Through the APB, set CRCCTRL.CRCBEATSIZE (8, 16 or 32 bits) and write CRCDATAIN; a 32-bit word takes 4 cycles, and new data may be written only while CRCSTATUS.CRCBUSY is clear.

Per-channel interrupt sources: Transfer Complete, Transfer Error and Channel Suspend, in CHINTFLAG, all ORed onto one NVIC line; INTSTATUS shows which channels have one and INTPEND gives the lowest such channel with its flags. Output event: CH, on block or beat completion. Input event actions: TRIG, CTRIG, CBLOCK, SUSPEND, RESUME, SSKIP, each enabled by CHCTRLB.EVIE; several may be on, and any enabled action follows any incoming event. In standby the DMAC is held off internally but keeps its settings. No synchronization is needed.

The EIC turns 8 external pins (EXTINT[7:0]) plus one non-maskable pin (NMI) into interrupt lines. Each line is maskable and senses rising, falling or both edges, or high or low level; each pin has a spike filter, can work asynchronously to wake from sleep with all clocks off, and can make an event. NMI behaves like the others but drives the CPU's non-maskable interrupt.

Pins are assigned through PORT. All interrupts are available in every sleep mode, though some can be set to stay masked to avoid waking. CLK_EIC_APB is set in the PM; GCLK_EIC, set up in GCLK, is needed for filtering and edge detection. There are two interrupt lines, EXTINT and NMI; NMI needs no NVIC set-up. Events are pulses. In debug halt the EIC keeps running. INTFLAG and NMIFLAG are not PAC-protected.

Order: enable CLK_EIC_APB; enable GCLK_EIC if edges or filtering are used; write EVCTRL, WAKEUP and CONFIGy; enable the EIC with CTRL.ENABLE. When NMI is used, enable GCLK_EIC after NMICTRL is set. CTRL.SWRST resets all registers and disables it.

CONFIGy.SENSEx sets edge or level sensing; a non-zero sense sets INTFLAG.EXTINT[x] when met. In edge mode a cleared flag sets again only on a new edge; in level mode it sets again at once if the level persists. CONFIGy.FILTENx turns on a majority filter that samples the pin three times on GCLK_EIC and passes the value two samples agree on. Level sensing without the filter is asynchronous and needs no GCLK_EIC; with filtering or edges the EIC requests GCLK_EIC itself. Detection delay depends on the mode.

NMI senses edges or level as set in NMICTRL.NMISENSE, with NMICTRL.NMIFILTEN for filtering. It is active by its sense setting alone, even with the EIC disabled, and has no detection after reset. A detection sets NMIFLAG.NMI, which always raises an interrupt request.

Sources: EXTINTx and NMI. EXTINTx are enabled one by one in INTENSET/INTENCLR and share one line; NMI has its own. EVCTRL.EXTINTEOx enables an event when a pin meets its CONFIGy condition. WAKEUP.WAKEUPEN[x] lets pin x wake the device; setting it with its interrupt disabled is not recommended. CTRL.SWRST and CTRL.ENABLE are synchronized on write (STATUS.SYNCBUSY); no register needs synchronization.

The NVM controller connects the flash to the AHB, for reads and writes, and to the APB, for commands and configuration. All NVM sections, calibration and configuration included, are memory-mapped. It has programmable read wait states, 16 individually lockable regions, extra boot loader protection, a security bit, power-down of flash blocks in sleep with optional wake on sleep exit or first access, and a direct-mapped cache.

It runs in any sleep mode with its clock running and its interrupt can wake the device. The PM puts the flash in low power on sleep entry according to CTRLB.SLEEPPRM. It uses CLK_NVMCTRL_AHB and CLK_NVMCTRL_APB; when the AHB frequency changes, the read wait states must suit it (the electrical characteristics give the numbers). In debug it keeps running; with the security bit set the flash is not reachable. INTFLAG and STATUS are not PAC-protected. After power-up it runs its own power-up sequence, holding AHB access, and then needs no set-up.

The flash is made of rows of four pages: erase is by row, write by page. A memory-mapped calibration and auxiliary space at NVM base + 0x00800000 holds factory calibration and system configuration and reads like main flash. A boot loader section can sit at the bottom of the main array (BOOTPROT fuses) and an EEPROM emulation area at the top (EEPROM fuses). The boot section is protected by its region lock bits and BOOTPROT; EEPROM rows stay writable whatever the region locks say.

The flash is split into 16 equal regions, each with a lock bit against write and erase; all are unlocked when shipped. The Lock and Unlock Region commands change the region holding the address in ADDR (written by software or left by the last write) until the next reset; LOCK shows the state. The power-up default is set by writing the user configuration in the auxiliary space with Write Auxiliary Page, effective after the next reset.

Reads and automatic page writes go straight to the mapped flash over the AHB; manual page writes, row erase and the rest are commands. A command is CTRLA.CMD written with the CTRLA.CMDEX key; INTFLAG.READY clears until it completes, and commands written meanwhile are ignored. CTRLB sets power reduction, read wait states and write mode. Reads return after CTRLB.RWS wait states.

Flash must be erased before it is written: the whole array by a debugger Chip Erase, or a row by Erase Row (all bits to one; refused with STATUS.LOCKE in a locked region; any address in the row will do). Data goes into a page-sized page buffer by 16- or 32-bit writes; 8-bit writes cause a system exception. Each write leaves its address in ADDR, and STATUS.LOAD shows the buffer has data. Automatic page write (MANW = 0, default) writes that page once its last word is loaded, and the row must be erased before that last write; partial pages need a manual write. Manual (MANW = 1): fill the buffer, then issue Write Page with CMDEX. While programming, INTFLAG.READY is low and AHB access stalls. The buffer resets to all ones after a page write; Page Buffer Clear empties a partial buffer. Set and Clear Power Reduction Mode commands move the controller and flash in and out of power reduction, shown by STATUS.PRM.

The Set Security Bit command locks the whole chip against external access; only a debugger Chip Erase clears it, and STATUS.PROGE can be checked after it. The cache is direct-mapped, 8 lines of 64 bits (64 bytes), enabled by clearing CTRLB.CACHEDIS, with three modes in CTRLB.READMODE; the INVALL command clears it, and commands that change flash invalidate it on their own. It saves power and helps speed when wait states are needed.

PORT drives the I/O pins in groups of up to 32. Each pin is general-purpose I/O or handed to a peripheral. As GPIO it is input or output with selectable drive strength and pull-up or pull-down, input sampling choice, and an input buffer that can be turned off to save power. Direction and output can be set, cleared or toggled atomically for any pins of a group in one 8-, 16- or 32-bit write. PORT sits on an AHB/APB bridge, and DIR, OUT and IN are also on the single-cycle CPU local bus (IOBUS).

Pins are named Pxy: x a group letter from A, y the bit 00 to 31. A selected peripheral function takes over the pad's output and can read it. During reset every pin is an input with input buffer, output buffer and pull all off. If PORT is powered down the pad latches keep output value and pull, but its registers and input synchronizers are lost and must be set up again. CLK_PORT_APB is set in the PM; PORT also runs on the CPU main clock for IOBUS access, which has priority over APB access, and its input synchronizers use that clock. No DMA, interrupts or events; it keeps running in debug halt. Choosing an analog function on a pin turns off its digital functions.

IOBUS connects the CPU straight to PORT at 0x60000000, with the same register map: single cycle, no wait states, byte, half-word or word access. DIR and OUT support read, write, set, clear and toggle there; IN is read only. As IOBUS cannot wait for resynchronization, pins read through it need continuous sampling turned on in CTRL.

DIR sets each pin as output (1) or input (0); OUT sets the level of an output. PINCFGy holds extra settings. IN reads the pin through a synchronizer, whatever the direction, unless PINCFGy.INEN is zero. A pin goes to a peripheral by setting PINCFGy.PMUXEN and writing its function in the PMUX register for that pin. After reset pins connect to PORT with outputs off and input buffers off, even with no clocks; debugger pins may differ.

Pin y's register set starts at PORT + (y / 32) × 0x80 and y % 32 is its bit. DIRSET/DIRCLR and OUTSET/OUTCLR/OUTTGL change single bits without touching other pins. IN is valid once PINCFGy.INEN is set. By default the input synchronizer runs only on a read, adding two CLK_PORT cycles; CTRL.SAMPLINGn keeps it running for a group of eight pins (n = (y % 32) / 8) at a power cost. PINCFGy is at offset PINCFG0 + (y % 32). The function is in PMUXn at offset PMUX0 + (y % 32) / 2: PMUXE (bits 3:0) for even y, PMUXO (bits 7:4) for odd y. The chosen peripheral must also be set up and enabled.

A pin can be totem-pole, open-drain or pulled, set in PINCFGy so no intermediate states appear when direction or value change. With the pull on, OUT picks pull-up (1) or pull-down (0). A totem-pole output drives the OUT level with no current limit beyond the pin's own; enabling the output driver turns off the pull. An input with no pull floats unless pulled outside.

The event system links peripherals directly: event generators emit signals that event users act on, with no CPU, bus or RAM involved. It has 6 channels, each able to take any generator and use an asynchronous, synchronous or resynchronized path; 18 generators; 44 users; configurable edge detection; SleepWalking and interrupts in low-power modes; software events. Each user picks which channel to listen to.

EVSYS can wake the CPU from every sleep mode even with its channel and bus clocks off. On a synchronous or resynchronized path a generator's event restarts that channel's generic clock GCLK_EVSYS_CHANNELx without waking the system, only for as long as needed (SleepWalking); an asynchronous path needs no clock. CLK_EVSYS_APB is set in the PM and each channel's generic clock must be set up in GCLK first. A software reset cancels events in progress. INTFLAG is not PAC-protected.

Set up generator and user peripherals first. Then the user, always before the channel: one 16-bit write to USER with the channel in USER.CHANNEL and the user in USER.USER. Then the channel: one 32-bit write to CHANNEL with CHANNEL.CHANNEL, PATH, EDGSEL and EVGEN. A setting is read back by an 8-bit write of USER.USER or CHANNEL.CHANNEL, then a read. EVSYS is always enabled; CTRL.SWRST resets it. Channels start with no generator (EVGEN = 0x00).

Asynchronous: the event passes straight from generator to user, even with the channel clock off; no interrupts, status or edge detection; lowest latency when generator and user share a generic clock. Synchronous: for a generator on the channel's own generic clock (otherwise events can be missed); interrupts and CHSTATUS work. Resynchronized: for a generator on another clock; the channel resynchronizes it; interrupts and CHSTATUS work. On the last two, CTRL.GCLKREQ = 0 requests the clock only to pass an event (SleepWalking) and 1 keeps it on.

Synchronous and resynchronized paths need edge detection: rising, falling or both (CHANNEL.EDGSEL); a pulse generator cannot use both. CHSTATUS.CHBUSYx is set while some user has not handled an event on channel x; CHSTATUS.USRRDYx is set when every user on it is ready.

Writing CHANNEL.SWEVT together with CHANNEL.CHANNEL fires an event on that channel. It needs a synchronous or resynchronized path (CHANNEL.PATH 0x0 or 0x1), rising-edge detection (CHANNEL.EDGSEL = 0x1) and CTRL.GCLKREQ = 0x1.

Per channel: Overrun (INTFLAG.OVRx), set when a user is not ready for a new event or an event arrives before all users handled the last; and Event Detected (INTFLAG.EVDx). Both work only on synchronous and resynchronized paths, share one line, and can wake the device from any sleep mode.
